content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

# Keeping the record

How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.

**history**
: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.

**pointer**
: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."

**pass**
: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.

## What an entry is

An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.

- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.

Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:

1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.

In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:

- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.

An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:

- keep: every check passes;
- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.

Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.

## Reading and writing

- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
- Commit the record file and its history together.
- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.

## The pass

Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.

The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.

1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.

Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.

## A consolidation

A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").

- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.

## The consolidation tools

Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Put the open questions of the runs on the review queue.

Pick the tool by the job:

- To bring the record in line with a landing: the record-landing workflow (`references/batch.md`, "The landing"). Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`.
- To find whether a POSITIONS entry comes from the curator's words or from an agent's summary or default: the mining workflow. Its writer changes only a sentence that is false, stale or not the curator's. Run it on the entries that it has not traced, before the clarity workflow rewrites them. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/README.md`.
- To make entries read on their own, with their meaning kept: the clarity workflow. For FACTS, it first judges every entry by the six checks of "What an entry is", and rewrites only those marked reword or reorganize. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/README.md`.
- To correct the entries that a review's findings name: the clarity workflow, with `findings.md` in each chunk's folder, in the form that its README gives. An entry changes only where a finding names it, and grows only by what the correction needs.
- To keep `fortress-repo`'s revival part short enough to read whole: the orientation workflow. Its update mode runs after each landing. Run its consolidate mode when a cold read or the regression quiz shows that the part no longer reads whole, or when an update cannot keep it within the README's budget. Its README: `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/README.md`.

## INDEX and the gap ledger

- Give each new note under `explorations/` one line in INDEX, from its header comment's first sentence.
- Put a run's working files in an `evidence/` folder beside its results file: its briefs, chunks and checks, and the worker reports that the results draw on. Move them there with `git mv` once the results are judged. Only the results file gets an INDEX line. `check-index.sh` skips evidence folders. Do not add a folder's name to its list to let the folder pass.
- The gap ledger keeps its rows in topic sections. A row keeps its number for good. `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` is the only way to write it. Other views, such as `explorations/apl/lessons.md`, are derived from it.
- Split a rewrite of the ledger among small workers, each with a slice of rows that it can hold. Run a duplicate search first, as its own step.
- Ask the curator before you regroup the ledger's rows or derive its views again.

Yes: a `FloatLiteral` is a `QQ` with the right to convert implicitly into every number type. Your other questions, in order.

**How the specification promises the conversion without declaring the type.** The Working Draft puts the numeral's value into its type. A numeral with a radix point has the type `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, 10, v\]`, where `n` is the digit count, `m` the digits after the point, and `v` the value of the digits read as an integer (`literals.tex:110-129`). So `3.125` has the type `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`, and any library type can declare a coercion from it that computes with `v` and `m`, exactly, at compile time. That is the promise: the coercion sees the digits. The Draft's own note says "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy. All the numeric/numeral types should be defined", and no library ever declared them (F-169). The prelude simplified it to one type, `FloatLiteral`, whose value is exact at run time instead of in the type. Haskell is the peer that built the Draft's idea: a literal reaches a user's type through `fromInteger` and `fromRational`, exactly. Swift's protocol hands a user's type a `Double`, which is why a `Decimal` written as a literal is inexact there, a known wart.

**The stress test you're after.** Three program-defined types, each declaring its own coercion from the literal types, run on both paths:
1. Complex: `3 + 4 i` and `3.78 + 3.243 i`, with `i` a constant of the type and juxtaposition as multiplication. Each component is a double, so the only question is one rounding. The prototype already has this case.
2. An interval, the Draft's example: a coercion that encloses the numeral's exact value between the two neighbouring doubles. It needs the exact value, not a double.
3. A reduced-precision float for machine learning, bfloat16 over a bit pattern: a numeral must round once from the exact value. Rounding first to a double and then to bfloat16 can land on the wrong neighbour. This is microGPT's own territory once we try smaller floats.

Under A all three get the exact literal by design. Under B, as stated, a program's type sees a double, so cases 2 and 3 lose. I've added 2 and 3 to the prototype, and asked it to find a numeral where the double rounding shows.

**Other types that would need it,** none in the library today: intervals; decimals, for money; bfloat16, float16 and float8, for ML; double-double or quad precision; fixed-point; arbitrary-precision floats; exact complex numbers over `QQ`; and dimensioned quantities, which the Draft specified with numerals and nobody built.

**The shape this points to,** my proposal, not yet costed: B at the places that fix no type, so `x = 3` is a `ZZ32` and no literal value lives at run time in ordinary code; and A for a program's own types, which may declare `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)` and receive the exact value, so a literal value exists at run time only as the argument of such a coercion, as in Haskell. I've asked the prototype worker to cost that hybrid by reading beside B: what the checker and the fold do differently, and which of the 24 glue bindings must stay for the literal's accessors.

You're not misreading what the Draft says about conversion; you're reading into it a rule it never states. Here is exactly what the text has and lacks.

**What it says:**
- "Literals are values; they do not require evaluation" (`literals.tex:25-26`). A numeral is a value, like `true` or `"ab"`.
- "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types because ... we expect them to be polymorphic ... numerals have their own types" (`:132-141`).
- "Libraries define coercions from numerals to integers (for simple numerals) and rational numbers (for compound numerals)" (`:146-148`).
- A quotient of two integer literals, and a numeral with an exponent, is a "static expression"; where one is used in a floating-point computation, "the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring at most one floating-point rounding error. But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time, not just at compile time" (`:166-175`).

**What it never says:** that a numeral may stand only where a type is declared, or that its type is gone at run time. The compile-time conversion it promises is for static expressions in a floating-point computation, one case. For `x = 3`, `Cell(3)`, `f(3)` at `Any`, or a bare `0.1` printed, the Draft gives no rule at all: its inference chapter is a heading and notes (F-169), and "polymorphic" is as far as it goes. In Fortress a value's type is a run-time thing, since dispatch reads it, so "numerals have their own types" with no further rule means that a numeral reaching such a place carries its numeral type at run time. That is what the prelude built as `FloatLiteral`, and what both paths do today.

**Your reading, made whole, is B.** "You never get a numeral at run time" needs one more sentence that the Draft lacks: where no type is declared, the compiler supplies one, `ZZ32` by size or `RR64`. With it, every numeral is converted at compile time, at the declared type or at the default, and the numeral types are the checker's alone. Without it, `x = 3` would be a static error, which no language accepts. So the design you've been describing is reading B with the fold, and the one addition I'd keep from the Draft's spirit is the hybrid for a program's own types, so that an interval or a bfloat16 can still receive the exact digits through its own coercion.

The Draft's authors leaned your way later: the 2012 restart gives a numeral an ordinary type, `QQ` or `NN`. They chose exact types as the default, where you'd choose the machine's.

Yes: a numeral is the written form, the digits in the source, such as `255`, `FF_16` or `1.1_2`. A number is the value it names. Two numerals can name one number: `255` and `FF_16`.

**Reading a numeral in a base.** Each digit position is a power of the base. Before the point the powers go up from the base to the power 0; after the point they go down: 1 over the base, 1 over the base squared, and so on. The base is 10 unless `_r` says otherwise.
- `255` is 2·100 + 5·10 + 5·1.
- `FF_16` is 15·16 + 15·1 = 255. In base 16 the digits run 0 to 9 then A to F, so F is 15.
- `0.5` in base 10 is 5 tenths. `0.25` is 2 tenths and 5 hundredths.
- `1.1_2` is 1·1 + 1·(1/2) = 1.5. The digit after the point is one half, because the base is 2.
- `C.8_16` is 12·1 + 8·(1/16) = 12.5.
- `0.1_16` is 1/16 = 0.0625.

Haskell does the second: `fromRational` hands the user's type a `Rational` at run time.

So "never at run time" holds for every built-in type, and for a program's own type the literal must appear once at run time, as the argument of its coercion, under any design. Here it is, step by step, with the terms first.

**Terms**
- **Numeral**: the digits written in the program, such as `3.14159` or `C.8_16`.
- **Compile time**: when the compiler reads the program and writes the class files.
- **Load time**: when the JVM loads a class file, once, before the program's code in it runs.
- **Run time**: when the JVM executes the program's code, each time the code is reached.
- **Coercion**: a conversion that the compiler inserts where a value of one type is used where another type is declared. Its body is library or program code.
- **Constant folding**: the compiler computes an expression at compile time and writes the result into the class file in place of the expression.

**What constant folding needs**
1. Every operand of the expression is a constant.
2. The compiler has the rule of the operation inside itself. It does not need to run any code of the program to get the result.
3. The result is a value that a class file can hold as a constant. A JVM class file holds five kinds: `int`, `long`, `float`, `double` and `String`.

**Cases that meet all three**
- `3 + 4`: the operands are numerals, the compiler knows `+` on integers, the result 7 is an `int`.
- `r: RR64 = 3.14159`: the operand is a numeral, the compiler knows how to round a rational to the nearest double, the result is a `double`.
- `q: QQ = 1/2`: the compiler knows rational arithmetic; the result is two integers, 1 and 2, which the class file holds.
- The prototype did these. This is the constant folding the Draft describes for "static expressions".

**The case that does not meet them**: `iv: Interval = 3.14159`, where `Interval` is a type that the program declares with its own `coerce`.
1. The operand is a constant. Met.
2. The operation is the body of the program's `coerce`. The compiler has no rule for it. The body is Fortress code: it can call functions, make objects, loop. To fold it, the compiler would have to execute Fortress code while compiling. No Fortress compiler can do that, the team's or ours. The only program that executes Fortress is walk. Not met.
3. The result is an `Interval` object. A class file cannot hold an object as a constant. Not met.

So this case is not constant folding. It is the same shape, but step 2 fails, and step 3 would fail even if step 2 passed. That is the whole difference: folding works where the compiler knows the operation, and a program's coercion is an operation the compiler does not know.

**What the Draft says.** It promises compile-time computation for static expressions: the quotient of two integer numerals, and a numeral with an exponent, converted to a float with one rounding (`literals.tex:166-173`). Those are built-in operations on numerals. It says that libraries define the coercions from numerals, and it does not say that the compiler executes a coercion's body. So the Draft asks for the folding the prototype did, and not for the folding of a program's coercion.

**The nearest the JVM allows for a program's type.** The compiler writes the numeral's four numbers as constants into the class file, and writes a call of the program's `coerce` with them into the class's initializer. The JVM runs that call once, at load time, and stores the result in a `static final` field. Every later use reads the field. The JIT treats the field as a constant. The body runs once per class, never per use.

**Where this leaves the two designs.** In both, the body gets the four numbers and runs once at load. In the hybrid they arrive as the fields of one argument. In the Draft's way they arrive as four static parameters, stamped into a class of their own per numeral. Same numbers, same single run, different plumbing. The hybrid needs no new kind of type and no class per numeral.

**The one way to get your full picture**, the object computed at compile time: give the compiler an evaluator for Fortress, which means running walk inside the compiler to execute coercion bodies, and then generating code that rebuilds the resulting object's fields at load time, since the file still cannot hold the object. That is compile-time execution of user code, Zig's `comptime`. It is a project of its own, and it would still end in a load-time construction of the object. Nobody has built it for Fortress.

What that means under the design:
- At a typed place, `z: ZZ32 = -3` is `-(3)` with `3` converted first. The compiled path already folds this: a prefix minus on a numeral becomes a negative constant before the checker (F-262 records that a numeral's sign does not reach its type).
- With the fold of expressions of literals alone, `-3`, `3 + 4` and `1/2` become one exact signed value before anything else, and that value converts or defaults like a numeral. One trap this avoids: `-2147483648`, the smallest `ZZ32`. Read as `-(2147483648)` with the default first, the inner numeral doesn't fit `ZZ32`, becomes a `ZZ64`, and the result is a `ZZ64`; Java has a special grammar rule for this one literal. Folding first gives the exact value, which fits `ZZ32`.
- For a program's own type, `c: CC64 = -3` is `-(3)`: the coercion receives the numeral `3` with its four numbers, and the type's own prefix `-` applies to the result. A type that cannot be negated refuses it, as it should.

**Ask 4: should the compiled path run a reduction's halves in parallel, and when?**

Primer:
- A reduction is `SUM`, `DOT` or `BIG MAX` over a range or an array. The library splits the range into two halves, computes each, and joins the two results: `red.join(loop'(lo, mid-1), loop'(mid, hi))` (`RangeInternals.fss:1320`). Both halves are the arguments of one call to `join`.
- Under walk the arguments of a call run in parallel, so each half forks and the reduction is a tree of tasks. On the compiled path the code generator evaluates a call's arguments one after another, under the team's own comment "Why isn't this parallel???" (`CodeGen.java:6935-6955`). Measured: 64 slow bodies in a `SUM` run at most one at a time, where a parallel `for` runs four. This is the defect the review calls N5.
- After the switch-over this hits microGPT directly: its whole gather is reductions, `SUM`, `DOT`, `BIG MAX` and the one-hot products, so every one of them would run in sequence on the compiled path. microGPT fast, phase 6, needs this fixed.
- The specification allows either: a call's arguments "may" be evaluated in parallel (`parallelism.tex:89-90`). The language's design, Steele's talks and walk, is parallel by default.
- Beside it, N1, a plain defect with no fork: a `do … also … end` group whose first arm throws does not wait for its other arms, so after the `catch` the other arms are still writing (`CodeGen.java:1662-1712`). Walk joins every arm. The fix is one code-generator rung: join all arms before the group completes abruptly. It is the first repair in the review's order, since an `IntegerOverflow` or an index fault in parallel numeric code otherwise leaves writers running. I'll put it in the batch after this one as a default; it needs no answer.

Options for N5:
1. **The code generator forks a call's arguments**, as it already forks the elements of a tuple, with `ParallelismAnalyzer` deciding which arguments are worth a task. This makes both paths evaluate arguments alike and fixes every reduction and every parallel call at once. One code-generator rung, plus a grain size in the one library's range split, which today splits down to single elements. Cost to watch: a task per argument where the analyzer doesn't prune.
2. **The one library's `generate` binds its two halves as a tuple**, which the code generator already forks. About one line in `RangeInternals.fss`, plus the grain size. Only reductions gain; other calls stay sequential on the compiled path, so walk and the compiled path keep differing on when arguments run in parallel.
3. **Leave reductions sequential** until PLAN's compiled-parallelism step in phase 6. Nothing now; microGPT's first compiled timing is sequential.

- P-174 **A numeral's own type is the Working Draft's, `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, both below `Numeral`, and its value carries the Draft's four numbers as fields; a program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from that type, which the compiler calls once per class, when the class loads.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`); they are fields of the value, not static parameters of the type, and the Draft's explicit-radix variants and `Literal[\v\]` fold into the radix field. The two types replace the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). A numeral type is written only as a parameter type, of a coercion or an operator, never as a variable's, field's or return type, so the library's `pi` and `e` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`) are `RR64`. A program's type declares the coercion inside itself, such as `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits the call with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171): in his words, "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral. Inside a coercion's body two numeral values compare by their reduced value, so `2.5` and `2.50` are equal there, under `SEQV` too (P-168). Fields cannot make a size static, so the design contradicts the binary chapter's static word width from a numeral's digit count (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1621`, `:1659-1662`), for Appendix I, and drops its `opr ||` with a numeral. Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`literals.tex:141-145`), as an interval type should receive `3.1415926535897932384` unrounded (`:135-141`). The team built that coercion under its own names, with the exact value in the numeral ("ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec", commit `128f313b5b`, 2009), but never the four numbers, and no team word calls the names temporary or final; the design keeps what they built, one type for each kind of numeral with its exact value at the coercion, and adds the Draft's names and numbers. The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). A coercion handed a double loses: a bfloat16 type then rounds `1.00390625000000000001` twice, to `0x3F80`, where one rounding gives `0x3F81`. P-173 weighs the bend of P-26. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1, 3 and 6; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`, sections 6 and 7.

The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is (F-335); `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals' 24 bindings, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, left the library with those two types (P-174), so no carrier is designed for them; `IntLiteral`'s other 8, its conversions and comparisons, left with it. A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run. Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. Detail: `reviews/natives-device-2026-11-07.md`, sections 3.1 to 3.4; the store's shape: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q2. 89:- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. The implicit coercion of `NN32` into `RR64`: P-75 holds it, with its conflict with the overloads of `RR64` and `ZZ64`. 91:- P-76 **An integer numeral has the Working Draft's type `NaturalNumeral` (P-174), which each of the eight number types converts from: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`.** Where nothing fixes a type it is a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-173). `NaturalNumeral` takes the place of `IntLiteral`, the name that the compiler's prelude and the interpreter's library give the type, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic goes, since an expression of numerals alone folds before the checker (P-173). Walk, before it runs the checker (P-12), converts an integer numeral from its exact value at each place that fixes a type, and elsewhere evaluates it at its default, which walk already gives it by its value (F-74). Walk gaps: coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511). 96:- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523). 99:- P-165 **`asFloat` and the `=` built on it leave `trait Number`; each built-in number type keeps its own `asFloat`.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32`, `RR64`, `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` (P-174) each declare `asFloat`, so the written conversion `asFloat(x)` into `RR64` is unchanged at every concrete type. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other (P-74); otherwise the program writes the conversion, `asFloat(x) = y`. The vector norm takes a bound that promises a float; its form is the default of a fork on his review list: the norm at each of the eight number types, each by its own `asFloat` (F-324). `Float`'s `^` at a `Number` exponent, `random`, `atan2` and `printThreadInfo` are declared at `RR64`, and coercion carries `ZZ32`, `RR32` and numerals to them. The specification's sentence follows (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex:56-73`). P-74's rule, an exact conversion implicit and a lossy one written, stands. Why: the team's compiler prelude declares `Number` with nothing in it (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:510`), and the specification does not ground the method: its sentence that names it on `Number` is the revival's revision. The curator's rule for such a case: an early idea of the interpreter's library goes where the specification does not ground it and the later prelude eliminated it. With `Number` open (P-160), an abstract `asFloat` would force a program's own number, such as a complex number, to invent a float, and `Number`'s `=` would compare two different complex numbers by it. 101:- P-168 **What `SEQV` means, on both paths: the specification's rule, with no special case for any type but the numeral types.** Values of different types are never strictly equivalent; two value objects of one type are when their fields are, tuples element by element and floats by their bit patterns; two reference objects are only when they are one object (`Specification/basic/objects.tex`, "Object Equivalence" and "Value Objects"). The one exception: two values of a numeral type inside a coercion's body are strictly equivalent when their reduced values are equal, so `2.5` and `2.50` are there (P-174). Both paths read the `value` modifier. Each path changes its own code: walk drops its equivalence across types (row 909) and its answer `true` for value objects whose body declares no field (row 113); the compiled helper `equality.sEquiv` gains the rule for value objects, tuples and floats (rows 906 and 907; the prelude's own `===` keeps row 908 until the switch-over). `ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects (P-166). Strings are reference objects: the library declares `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` without `value`, so two such strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and text equality is the strings' own `=`; P-171 makes two literals of one text one object. This overrules the team's code on both paths, walk's `seqv` and the prelude's `opr ===(a:String, b:String) = a=b`, where the specification is silent on strings. A program with a `value object CC64` tests it on both paths beside the review's 14 cases (F-326). Why: the specification's rule read as written, over the team's unfinished code of 2008 and 2010, which its authors called preliminary and incomplete; P-167 makes this one comparison that both paths answer. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4; `reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md`, sections 3 and 7. 103:- P-172 **A numeral with a radix point has the Working Draft's type `RadixPointNumeral` (P-174), which holds the numeral's exact value: `QQ` converts from it exactly, and `RR64` and `RR32` with one rounding.** So `3.125` converts to the `QQ` value `3125/1000`, `q: QQ = 0.5` binds and `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`; into `RR64` or `RR32` a numeral rounds once, to the type's nearest value, on both paths. `QQ`, `RR64` and `RR32` each declare the pair of `=` that goes with each coercion (P-165). Where nothing fixes a type the numeral is an `RR64` (P-173): `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`, and a bare numeral prints as that double, so `"" 2.50` is `"2.5"`, and the team's `tests/NumberPrintTest.fss:16`, which asserts that a numeral prints as written, changes. `RadixPointNumeral` stands beside the number types, as the compiler's prelude declares its `FloatLiteral` (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:996`), in place of the interpreter library's `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` (`FortressBuiltin.fsi:44` at `b430f9f42`). Walk converts such a numeral from its exact value where its place fixes a type, at a binding, a parameter, a field and a declared return type, so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `0.25 + 0.25`. The specification's literals chapter and the coercions of `basic-lib/numbers.tex:43` follow, with an Appendix I entry, in the revision form (P-96). A numeral at `round`, `floor`, `ceiling` or `truncate` converts into `RR64` by P-173's reading of a tie among `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64`, so one within half an ulp of a tie rounds as its nearest double, not as the rational: `round(2.50000000000000001)` is 2. No line of microGPT changes, and by reading its numerals keep their bits. Why: the Working Draft keeps a numeral unconverted, since "converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision", gives 3.125 "the rational value 3125/1000", has the library coerce a compound numeral to the rationals, and converts a static rational expression into a float with "at most one floating-point rounding error" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-173`); the curator reads it so: nothing is lost in `QQ`, and a float of fixed size takes one rounding. 104:- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174), or is a numeral type; `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types' names and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`. 105:- P-174 **A numeral's own type is the Working Draft's, `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, both below `Numeral`, and its value carries the Draft's four numbers as fields; a program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from that type, which the compiler calls once per class, when the class loads.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`); they are fields of the value, not static parameters of the type, and the Draft's explicit-radix variants and `Literal[\v\]` fold into the radix field. The two types replace the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). A numeral type is written only as a parameter type, of a coercion or an operator, never as a variable's, field's or return type, so the library's `pi` and `e` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`) are `RR64`. A program's type declares the coercion inside itself, such as `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits the call with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171): in his words, "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral. Inside a coercion's body two numeral values compare by their reduced value, so `2.5` and `2.50` are equal there, under `SEQV` too (P-168). Fields cannot make a size static, so the design contradicts the binary chapter's static word width from a numeral's digit count (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1621`, `:1659-1662`), for Appendix I, and drops its `opr ||` with a numeral. Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`literals.tex:141-145`), as an interval type should receive `3.1415926535897932384` unrounded (`:135-141`). The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). A coercion handed a double loses: a bfloat16 type then rounds `1.00390625000000000001` twice, to `0x3F80`, where one rounding gives `0x3F81`. P-173 weighs the bend of P-26. **Terms.** A numeral is the digits written in the source: `3`, `0.5`, `C.8_16`. Its four numbers: `n` the digit count, `m` the digits after the point, `r` the radix, `v` the digits read as one integer. A static parameter is what sits in a type's brackets, like the `16` in `Array[\RR64, 16\]`: the compiler knows it; it never changes while the program runs.

- "A numeral containing only digits ... has type `NaturalNumeral[\n, 10, v\]`"; with a radix point, "`RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, 10, v\]`"; "Every numeral also has type `Numeral[\n, m, r, v\]`".
- "Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types because ... we expect them to be polymorphic. For example, consider the numeral `3.1415926535897932384`; converting it immediately to a floating-point number may lose precision. If that numeral is used in an expression involving floating-point intervals, it would be better to convert it directly to an interval. Therefore, numerals have their own types."
- "This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations."
- "the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring at most one floating-point rounding error."

**Your design, reflected back**

1. A numeral has a type at compile time only: `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, below `Numeral`, with the four numbers as static parameters. `3.125` has the type `RadixPointNumeral[\4, 3, 10, 3125\]`. The parser gives the compiler the four numbers; the checker carries them in the type. These types live in the checker. When the program runs there is no numeral object, no method on one, nothing of the numeral left. `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` are gone.

2. Where a type is fixed, the compiler converts the numeral at compile time, from the exact value. Constant folding. Into an integer type exactly, or a refusal at compile time when it does not fit. Into `QQ` exactly. Into `RR64` or `RR32` with one rounding. The class file holds the finished constant. Walk gives the same value at the same place.

3. Your own number type gets numerals by declaring a coercion whose parameter is the numeral type, generic over the four numbers. The Draft's interval, as the coordinator showed you at 21:35:

   ```

Its body is a call of your type's constructor with values computed from `n, m, r, v`. The compiler knows the four numbers, so it instantiates the coercion for that numeral and emits the constructor call with the constants. The result is a constant of the program: one object per site, computed once. No double in between. The one JVM detail you accepted at 22:21: a class file cannot hold an object as a constant, so that object is built once when the class loads, into a `static final` field, and every use reads it.

**How constant folding is built.** It is a compiler pass over the syntax tree (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java`, phase 4 of the phases). It looks for an expression whose operands are all numerals and whose operator is one of a fixed list (`+ - * / ^`, unary `-`, the comparisons). It computes the result itself, in Java, with exact integer and rational arithmetic, and replaces the expression by one constant node. It never calls the library's `opr +`. javac does the same: `1 + 2` in Java source becomes `3` in the class file, and the compiler's knowledge of `+` is its own.

So yes, it is knowledge the compiler has. But look at what it knows: how to read digits in a radix as an exact number, and what `+ - * /` mean on exact numbers. That is the meaning of numerals, which the language defines, not the meaning of any library type. The Draft says it in those terms: "the quotient of two integer literals is a static expression whose value is rational", and "the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then converts the result". No library type is involved until the conversion.

**Where the compiler must know a library type.** At the conversion into a built-in type: to turn the exact `1/2` into the double `0.5` in the class file, the compiler must know that `RR64` is the JVM's `double` and `ZZ32` its 32-bit `int`. It knows that already: these types are `native`, their bodies are `builtinPrimitive` calls, and the code generator carries them as JVM primitives. That is knowledge of representation, not of behaviour. Under your design `ZZ32` still declares its coercion from `NaturalNumeral` in the library, in the same generic form as `Interval` does; the compiler's fold is an optimization of that declared coercion, and it must give the same value. That is testable: run the library's coercion under walk, compare with the compiled constant. If they ever differ, it is a defect. So the shipped types go through the one mechanism, and the compiler shortens it where the result is a JVM primitive. Every compiler on the JVM does that much; the JVM has primitives, and nothing else is a constant there.

**For your own type** the compiler cannot run the body, so the constructor call runs once at class load. Same meaning, later moment. One thing the fold gives built-in floats that your type does not get for free: `r: RR64 = 0.1 + 0.2` folds to the exact `3/10` and rounds once, so `r` is the double nearest `0.3`, not `0.30000000000000004` as `0.1 + 0.2` on doubles gives. That is the Draft's "at most one rounding error", and it exists only where the compiler folds.

**Point 2, now.** `-3`, `10/20` and `0.1 + 0.2` are all expressions over numerals. At your own `Interval`, what is `iv: Interval = 10/20`? Three readings:

1. Your type's own operators on the coerced numerals: `coerce(10) / coerce(20)` with `Interval`'s `/`, at run time. This is how `3 + 4 imaginary` works for `CC64`, and how repair 3 treats the sign: `-3` is `-(coerce(3))` with your type's `-`.
2. Fold first, exactly. The value `1/2` is a rational, so its type is `QQ`, and `Interval` takes it only through a coercion from `QQ`, which an interval type would want anyway. Exactness is kept for everyone. But then `-3` at `CC64` would be the exact integer `-3`, of type `ZZ`, and `CC64` would need `coerce(x: ZZ)`.
3. Fold first, then hand your coercion a numeral made from the result's digits. It breaks on `1/3`, which has no digits.

Repair 3, as you took it at 23:23, is a mix: reading 1 for the sign ("a negative constant reaches it as the prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result"), reading 2 for everything else ("a quotient as `QQ`"). The sign is special for a reason: a numeral has no sign, and negation is the additive group's operation that every number type has, so `-3` at your type costs you nothing extra. The other operators on numerals are static expressions, their values are exact, and exact values have exact types, `ZZ` and `QQ`.

The question is whether that mix is what you want: the sign through your type's `-`, every other static expression through a coercion from `QQ` or `ZZ`. A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of digits)
has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is the value of the numeral
interpreted in radix ten.  If the numeral has no leading zeros, or is
the literal \EXP{0}, then it also has type \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}.
\note{Can the type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}
have any value other than what you get from evaluating the corresponding literal?

What is the relationship between \EXP{\TYP{Literal}\llbracket{}v\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n, 10, v\rrbracket}?

We need to describe the \TYP{Numeral} type hierarchy.
All the numeric/numeral types should be defined and their relations to each other given.
And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
}

\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
Or is that just part of lexical structure?
(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
where $v$ is
the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point) has type
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
interpreted in radix ten.

A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
be the radix) has the following type:
\begin{Fortress}
\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
\end{Fortress}
where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.

Every numeral also has type
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.


Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
because, as in common mathematical usage,
we expect them to be polymorphic.
For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
converting it immediately to a floating-point number
may lose precision.
If that numeral is used in an expression
involving floating-point intervals,
it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
in Fortress).
\Library\ define coercions
from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
and rational numbers (for compound numerals).


\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
this is true regardless of whether
the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
Fortress.

\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
is a static expression whose value is rational.
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

FACTS.md:199
- F-129 **A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`, and a program whose sizes are known at compile time loads, dispatches and runs compiled, apart from the open cases below.** It builds P-41. Each size value, such as the 3 of `Vec[\3\]`, has one descriptor; in a run-time subtype test, it is a supertype only of an equal size. A size read as a value is a constant that the class loader replaces by the numeral. Closures and tasks capture a size as a free static parameter (F-135). A size made from a number known only at run time does not run compiled: `tests/NatReflectTest.fss` stops at load (row 307). Gated by `compiler_tests/NatRt*`. Also open on the compiled path: a `ZZ32Vector` passed to a generic constructor fails at load (row 408); a dispatched overload arm whose static parameter has a concrete generic bound stops the compile in its sized form and dies at load in its type form (row 413); an object that extends two instantiations of one trait, one at a static parameter, passes the checker and dies at load (row 414). Row 416 is walk's defect: walk refuses at load `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, which the compiled run dispatches, since walk's overloading check applies no exclusion of instantiations. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 9.

FACTS.md:246
- F-340 **On the compiled path a numeral at a typed place of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` or `RR32` is that type's constant, a float rounded once, and a program's coercion from a numeral runs once per site, in the component class's static initializer.** The coercion desugarer types the numeral at the place's type (`compiler/desugarer/CoercionDesugarer.scala`), and the code generator emits the type's `make` with a float from `roundToDouble` or `roundToFloat` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java`), so `x: RR64 = 0.9999999999999999` is below 1.0; each site's coercion result is a static field `numeral$coercion$N` of the component's class, and a coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A program's generic type is not hoisted (row 957). Tests: `compiler_tests/FloatNumeralOneRounding.test`, `NumeralCoercionOnceCompiled.test`, `NumeralCoercionRaisesCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-literal-fold/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".
